title: Monthly climate explained the WWII-drought runoff surplus but not the 1946-1956 surplus; the Millennium Drought fell 12-16% below a monthly model at 16 south-east Australian gauges (1889-2025)
abstract:
Question: in long BoM flow records, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff at equal annual rain was above the annual rainfall-runoff relation during the WWII drought (1937-1945), high in 1946-1956, low in the 1960s-1990s and low after 1997. Earlier tests used the annual relation Q = a + bP + cP(t-1). Does a monthly water-balance model driven only by monthly rain and PET, calibrated in 1957-1996, reproduce these departures out of sample?

Approach: 16 SE-AU gauges, 7 cells (BoM daily flow 1890-2025), SILO monthly rain from 1889, CRU TS 4.09 PET. GR2M calibrated per gauge (KGE). Per year: departure from the annual relation, climate part (GR2M minus annual relation) and remaining departure (observed minus GR2M), in % of mean 1957-1996 runoff; cell bootstrap. The plan preceded all model runs. A volume-bias correction was added post hoc; both versions are reported.

Results: the WWII-drought surplus (+16.8%, 95% CI +10.0 to +23.3) was a climate effect (climate part +18.2%; remaining -1.4%, -12.8 to +11.4). The 1946-1956 surplus (+27.8%) was not (climate part -1.6%; remaining +29.4%, +9.1 to +43.6); the North control had the same high. In 1997-2009 the model expected a surplus of about +10%, but runoff was 3-6% below the annual relation: the remaining departure was -12.4% (-24.1 to -2.3), or -15.7% with a pre-1997 calibration, below every cross-validated pre-1997 13-year block (-10.5 to +19.1). At the same 10 gauges it was 9.9 points (2.9 to 19.5) below the WWII drought at equal rain deficit. GR2M variants gave -12 to -20%; abcd gave -4 to -10%. Monthly climate gives a 2010-2025 decline of 8-9% (less cool-season rain, higher PET). With SILO rain the remaining 2010-2025 departure was small (+2.0%, or -3.4%, -18.9 to +2.5); with AGCD rain (2010-2022) it was -10 to -14% (CIs below 0). Baseflow and quickflow changed in proportion.

Conclusion: there is no single multi-decadal efficiency cycle with a monthly-climate cause. The WWII-drought surplus is a climate effect of the annual relation's dry-year bias; the 1946-1956 high is not climatic in these data and occurred in both regions; against a monthly model the Millennium Drought is the period below all earlier variation. Whether runoff stayed below its climate expectation after 2010 depends on the rain product.

Limitations: 16 gauges in 7 cells; a two-parameter model that misses wet-year curvature; post hoc bias correction; early ratings and PET not tested; SILO-AGCD difference unresolved; land use not tested.

We use its 58 long-record gauges, BoM flow and SILO recipes, and its annual relation. We support its finding of a pre-1957 high, but challenge its reading of the WWII drought: a monthly model gives the WWII-drought surplus from climate alone, and against that model the Millennium Drought is the anomaly.

Context from earlier campaign work on the post-1997 runoff deficit: Mainland south-east Australian catchments protected before 1997 lost about as much runoff after 1997 as unprotected ones; four wet Tasmanian catchments made the planned opposite result (175 basins)

Same gauge set and block design. We support its finding that measured climate does not explain the 1941-1953 high, now with a monthly water-balance model, and we extend its cool-season result: monthly climate predicts most of the 2010-2025 decline with SILO rain.
